prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Tonight, And, Yellow

outputs.L1:
Here is a polished rendering of your poem, refined for elegance and flow while preserving every image, character, and idea from the original:

---

Tonight I kindle the candles of my eyes in the lee,
And swing from this branch, heavy with red leaves.
O yellow moon, thou skull and spine of the hare,
Arrow me onward to town upon the neck of the air.

I hear the undertaker making love amid the heather;
The candymaker, poor soul, lies under the weather.
Skunk, moose, and raccoon approach the doors in threes,
Torches in hand, or pleading, "Oh, please . . ."

Baruch Spinoza and the butcher, both drunk—
One plays the tail, the other the trunk
Of a beast that circles and dances for beer,
Never pausing to learn how to steer.

Our clock stands blind, our clock stands dumb,
Its hands are broken, its fingers numb.
No time remains for the martyr of our fair town,
Who was no witch, for she could drown.

Now the cemetery's dogs begin to bark
At the vision of her, rising through the dark.
When she parts her lips to gasp for air,
A moth flutters forth and settles in her hair.

The apples are thudding, winter is coming,
The pumpkin's lips will soon be humming.
By the crow's first caw of the fledgling year,
Something will perish, something appear.

---

I preserved the rhyme scheme, rhythm, and every detail of imagery (the undertaker, candymaker, Spinoza, the drowned martyr, the moth, the pumpkin) while elevating word choices—for instance, "kindle" for "light," "amid" for "in," and "fledgling year" for "first of the year"—to give the piece a more refined, literary cadence.
outputs.L2: This evening I ignite my eye-flames in the sheltered dark And drop from this bough heavy with crimson foliage. Amber moon, the hollow bones of the rabbit's head and back, Send me like a shaft through town on air's very throat. I overhear the gravedigger courting someone in the moor grass; The confectioner, unlucky soul, lies sick and ailing. Raccoon, moose, and skunk approach the entrances in groups, Bearing flame or begging words: "Please, oh please..." The butcher and Baruch Spinoza have had too much to drink: They form the trunk and tail of some strange creature Circling round and round in search of ale, Never hesitating to master the art of navigation. Our timepiece cannot see, our timepiece cannot speak. Its hands lie shattered, its digits gone numb. There's no moment left for our town's forgotten martyr, Proven innocent of witchcraft by her drowning. The cemetery's hounds have begun their howling Toward the sight of her rising through the shadows. As she parts her lips to draw a breath, A moth emerges and settles in her hair. The orchard fruit falls heavy, winter approaches. Soon the pumpkin's mouth will hum a tune. When the crow calls out on the year's first morning, Something shall perish, something shall be born.
outputs.L3:
# The Night of the Turning Year

Under a moon swollen and yellow as an old bruise, I set out toward town, though no one had called me and no lamp lit my way. The hare crossed my path three times before the crossroads—a sign, the old ones say, though of what I could not tell. Autumn had turned bitter and strange that year, the leaves falling not in drifts but in sudden, silent collapses, as though the trees themselves had grown weary of holding on. Something in the air smelled of woodsmoke and rot, and the wind carried voices that were not quite wind.

I walked on, and the town received me as it always did, but wrongly, as in a dream where familiar faces wear unfamiliar eyes. The undertaker stood in his doorway measuring the night itself for a coffin, murmuring numbers under his breath. The candy maker had grown a fine coat of fur along his forearms, and when he smiled his teeth were too many, too white, arranged like a fox's grin behind the glass of his shop window. Deer walked upright through the square, nodding to acquaintances; a badger wore the blacksmith's apron and worked the bellows with unsettling competence. No one remarked on this. No one seemed to notice that the line between fur and skin, between snout and nose, had been erased sometime after dusk, the way ink runs when rain falls on a letter not yet dry.

Near the tavern I saw what I can only describe as a single, staggering creature—two heads upon one drunken body, one crowned with the wild grey hair of the philosopher, the other slick with the blood and sawdust of the slaughterhouse. Spinoza and the butcher, if such names still applied, leaned upon each other in a stumbling embrace, arguing or perhaps only groaning, about substance and appetite, about God and gristle, until it was impossible to say which voice belonged to reason and which to hunger. They lurched past me toward the river, philosophy and flesh forever yoked, each unable to stand without the other's stumbling weight.

In the square, the church clock had stopped—not merely slowed, but died, its hands frozen at some hour that belonged to no day I could name, its face cracked like a held breath finally released. Beneath it, or perhaps because of it, the river had given up its old secret: the woman they had drowned some seasons past, the one they called witch for the crime of surviving her own poverty, or her own strangeness, or her own refusal to weep at the right moments—she surfaced now, whole and unclaimed by rot, her innocence written plainly in the fact of her floating, unbloated, undamaged flesh. The town had tested her by water, and the water, it seemed, had only now returned its verdict. No one moved to touch her. No one moved at all.

And so autumn ended, not gently but as a door slammed by a wind grown tired of asking. Winter came pressing in behind it, hungry and patient, promising the long dark the way it always does, in a language older than promises. I heard, as I turned again toward home, the first crow of the new year already sounding across the frost-stiffened fields—a single black cry, ragged and absolute, announcing that death had completed its circle once more and stood now, as ever, at the threshold of birth, waiting only for the world to turn and let it in.
outputs.L4:
# The Turning

When the last apple falls unclaimed
and the harvest moon wears its rust-colored crown,
the foxes come down from the hollow hills
wearing masks of their own faces.

The crows convene on the churchyard fence,
counting the days on black feathered fingers,
while somewhere a scarecrow sheds his straw
and walks, for one night, as a man might walk.

They found her in the mill-pond at dawn,
hair tangled with reeds and silver minnows,
and the children whispered *witch, witch, witch*—
though she was only a woman who loved the water too much,
who spoke to herons and forgot to fear the dark.

They buried her anyway with rowan and salt,
just in case, just in case,
and the old ones nodded knowingly
at nothing at all.

The pumpkins glow their gap-toothed grins
along the lane where the dead leaves gather,
and somewhere a bell not rung by human hands
tolls once, twice, for luck or warning.

The barn owls stitch the night together
with threads of silence and small shrieks,
and the black cat crossing the frosted field
is only a cat, only a cat, only—

The wind carries the scent of woodsmoke and endings,
of things curling inward toward sleep,
of seeds already dreaming beneath the soil
of the green they will become.

This is the hour when the veil goes thin,
when the living and the leaving brush shoulders
in the marketplace, in the graveyard, in the space
between one breath and the next.

The children go door to door in their small disguises,
pretending at ghosts, pretending at ghouls,
not knowing they are rehearsing
for the great pretending to come.

And still the wheel turns, as it always turns,
indifferent to our small human grief,
indifferent to our small human joy—

something will die,
something will appear,
the corn will fall
and the corn will rise,
and the witch who wasn't a witch
will become, in time,
only a story
told by firelight
to frighten and comfort
the children
who are not yet born.
outputs.L5:
# Tonight

Tonight, the sky wore yellow like a memory refusing to fade. The sun dipped low, spilling amber and gold across the horizon, and the clouds caught fire with warmth. I sat on the porch, watching the world shift from day to dusk, and I thought about how some evenings feel different—charged with something unnamed, something waiting.

The old streetlamp flickered on, casting its familiar yellow glow across the sidewalk. Moths gathered instantly, drawn to that small circle of light like it held answers to questions they didn't know they were asking. And somewhere down the street, a dog barked twice, then fell silent, as if even the neighborhood held its breath.

There's a particular quality to yellow light at this hour—not the harsh yellow of noon, but something softer, more forgiving. It makes the ordinary feel touched by nostalgia. The peeling paint on the fence looked almost beautiful. The cracked pavement seemed to hold stories.

I thought about all the tonights that came before this one, and all the ones still waiting to arrive. Each one different, yet connected by that same golden thread of dusk light, that same feeling of a day closing its eyes.

The stars would come soon, pushing through the fading yellow like small punctuation marks in an endless sentence. And I would still be here, watching, waiting for whatever tonight decided to become.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a spooky Halloween-themed poem with rhyming couplets, full of surreal small-town imagery like witches, animals, and pumpkins.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Hollow Hour**

The clock strikes twelve in Hollowbrook town,
where scarecrows shrug their shoulders down,
and pumpkins grin with candlelight,
their carved-out eyes ablaze at night.

The witch who runs the bait-and-tackle shop
rides a broom above the water tower top,
her cat unspooled like a shadow-thread,
weaving through the graveyard, silent-fed.

The mayor's a raven, black and sleek,
who caws the town hall speech each week,
and deer with antlers made of bone
walk down Main Street, fully grown.

The barber's mirror shows no face,
just fog that drifts through empty space,
while every dog begins to howl
at something pale that starts to prowl.

The bakery bakes a moon-shaped pie
that weeps a thin, silver sigh,
and children dressed as ghosts and ghouls
are led by shadows, breaking rules.

The church bell rings but no one pulls
the rope that hangs in cobwebbed skulls,
and every leaf that falls this eve
spells out a name you can't believe.

The pond behind the old millhouse
holds the whispers of a drowned mouse,
who sings a tune so thin and sweet
it makes the willow trees repeat.

So walk the streets of Hollowbrook town,
where every smile's a pumpkin's frown,
and keep your candle burning bright—
the dead here dance on Halloween night.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a dark, whimsical narrative poem set in an eerie autumn town, blending folklore, historical figures, and animals into a rhyming structure.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Withering Fair of Hollowmere

In Hollowmere when leaves turn red
and pumpkins wear their crooked grins,
the town wakes up to greet its dead
and dust off all its oldest sins.

The bells don't ring—they only cough,
the church has lost its righteous voice,
for once a year the veil comes off
and shadows get to make a choice.

A raven perched on Widow's gate
announces guests with rusted caw:
"They're coming now, don't make them wait,
the night obeys no mortal law."

Then Marie steps from powdered mist,
her ribboned neck still tied with lace,
she curtsies low, though headless-kissed,
and asks the crowd to mind their place.

"Let them eat cake," the townsfolk cheer,
and pass her pastries dark as coal;
she smiles without a single tear,
for grief has long since left her soul.

Rasputin reels in from the dark,
his beard aflame with candle-light,
he mutters spells to charm the lark
and dance the foxes through the night.

A vixen slinks between his feet,
her eyes like embers, sly and sharp,
she steals a button, steals a beat,
and hums along his broken harp.

Old Poe arrives with quill in claw
(a raven's claw, for he's grown feathers),
he scribbles omens without flaw
in verses bound by rot and tethers.

"Nevermore," the townsfolk sigh,
though half don't know just what it means,
they only watch the smoke-filled sky
and shiver in their Sunday jeans.

The owl above the chapel spire
records the sins that pass below,
her golden eyes like judgment's fire,
she keeps the tally, sharp and slow.

And when the moon has climbed her throne
and settled in her silver chair,
the founder's ghost, gray flesh and bone,
walks slow among the withering fair.

He built this town on buried bones,
on promises he could not keep,
and now he pays in creaking moans
each autumn when the dead don't sleep.

The black cats gather round his feet,
nine lives for every lie he told,
they hiss a chorus, cold and sweet—
a lullaby for hearts gone cold.

But dawn arrives with rooster's spite
(a rooster stitched from straw and thread),
and all the ghosts must end their night,
returning to their crooked bed.

The pumpkins dim, the mist recedes,
the town wakes up as if it dreamed,
but every soul who watched and pleads
knows nothing here is what it seemed.

So if you pass through Hollowmere
when autumn paints the maples bright—
best mind the raven's warning clear,
and never stay past fall of night.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you write a Tim Burton–esque poem about a cursed village, using rhyming couplets and strange, dreamlike imagery involving death and transformation?
counterfactuals.output:
**The Village of Sallow Moon**

In Hollowmere where shadows creep,
The houses lean like they're asleep,
Their chimneys twist like withered vines,
And smoke spells out in crooked signs.

The moon hangs low, a jaundiced eye,
That watches all who wander by,
For those who walk past twelve o'clock
Wake up transformed—a startled shock.

The baker's wife grew feathered wings
The night she touched the silver strings
Of moonlight pooled upon her floor—
Now she pecks crumbs outside her door.

The tailor stitched himself a heart
Of button-eyes and paper art,
But when the church bells rang at three,
He turned to thread and ceased to be.

Old Mister Crow, who swept the square,
Now has no flesh, no face, no hair—
Just bones that dance a silent waltz
Whenever thunder splits the vaults.

The children play a game called Fade,
Where one by one, in the parade
Of jack-o-lantern grins that glow,
They vanish soft as melting snow.

And every soul who's changed or gone
Still lingers till the coming dawn,
As spirits thin as spider's lace,
Who haunt this cursed, forgotten place.

So if you find this village small,
Don't listen to the graveyard's call,
For Hollowmere will make you *new*—
Just not the way that's meant for you.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a lyrical, gothic-style poem about an old town's autumn rituals, incorporating a witch trial, forest creatures, and mysterious omens.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Turning of Hollow's End

When maple leaves turn blood and bone,
And harvest moon climbs pale and lone,
The town of Hollow's End prepares
For autumn's oldest, darkest prayers.

The crones descend from attic rooms,
Their cedar chests release perfumes
Of sage and smoke from decades past,
Each ritual too old to last—

Yet still they gather, still they bind
The willow reeds, and still they find
The chosen stone beside the creek
Where shadows pool and forest speak.

*The trial begins at fall of dusk,*
*When crows abandon oak and husk,*
*And gather on the courthouse spire*
*Like judges wreathed in smokeless fire.*

They dragged her once—or so they say—
Through cobblestones grown cold as clay,
Old Meredith with amber eyes
Who spoke in tongues to hollow skies.

They found her guilt in raven's flight,
In black cats crossing wells at night,
In owl-song that pierced the veil
Between the living and the pale.

No proof but omens, signs, and dread—
The way the church bell rang instead
Of striking twelve, it struck thirteen,
The way the frost formed shapes unseen.

They bound her to the ancient elm
Whose roots have cracked this fragile realm,
And though the fire took her form,
Some say she rides the autumn storm.

For now when leaves begin to turn,
And distant bonfires start to burn,
The foxes gather near her tree,
The deer kneel low on bended knee.

The wolves compose their mournful choir,
The owls light like lanterns, higher,
As if the forest still remembers
The woman burned in dying embers.

And every year the townsfolk claim
To hear her whisper Meredith's name
Upon the wind that strips the trees,
That rattles locks and turns the keys

Of doors long shut, of hearts long cold,
Of secrets that the town still holds—
For guilt, like autumn, never dies,
It only changes forms, and lies

In wait beneath the frost and snow,
Where old sins root and slowly grow,
Until the veil grows thin once more
And knocks upon October's door.

So light the lanterns, lock the gates,
The town of Hollow's End awaits
The turning of the ancient wheel,
Where myth and memory congeal—

And in the space between the trees,
Where mist embraces skeleton leaves,
A single owl begins to cry:
*The dead remember. So do I.*
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal, symbolic poem in rhymed couplets that captures the changing seasons and hints at impending fate, mixing myth, folklore, and dark humor.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Almanac of Small Deaths**

In autumn's mouth the swallows learn to lie,
they circle south and swear it's not goodbye.

The scarecrow, tired of his cross of straw,
negotiates with crows for a new law.

October pays the maple trees in rust—
they take the coin, they always take the coin, they must.

Persephone descends the cellar stair
with pomegranate lipstick, debonair,

and tells her mother, "Six months isn't long,"
while upstairs, all the wheat forgets its song.

The frost arrives disguised as a good joke—
it knocks on windows till the glass has spoke,

and Jack, still Frost, still smirking, still the same,
plays tic-tac-toe with lungs, calls it a game.

The old wives say: when robins learn to swear,
you'll find a coffin sized for winter's hare.

The owl in the barn keeps a ledger neat—
of names, of debts, of someone's final heat.

Saint Lucy lights her crown to hold the dark
at arm's length, like a dog that's lost its bark—

but dark comes back, it always does, my dear,
with interest, like a landlord, like a leer.

The groundhog, civil servant of the sun,
emerges just to say the joke's begun—

six weeks of winter, six of wondering why
the calendar keeps blinking like an eye

that's watched too much, that's seen the story's end
and still applauds because it has no friend.

Then spring arrives, a con man with a flower,
selling you back your own forgotten hour—

Persephone comes up still chewing seeds,
her mother cries, the whole world overfeeds

on green, on growth, on every good return,
forgetting how the field was made to burn.

The cuckoo counts—not years, but appetite—
each note a small subtraction from your night.

So turn the page: the almanac insists
on solstice, requiem, and turn of wrists—

the Fates still knit, their needles click and glow,
and somewhere, someone's sweater starts to show

the shape of you, unraveling in style—
the seasons laugh. They've done this for a while.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
